collections.label: The Bible, the Room and the Season Order
Format Rights, the Remake and the Territory

entries.name: The Episodic Series
entries.description: A series built as self-contained episodes, each resolving what it opens, so the run can be watched in any order.
entries.principle: Episodic construction is a rerun and syndication strategy as much as a story shape — each episode has to stand alone because stripped rerun scheduling requires it to be sellable and watchable out of sequence. The form favours a repeatable engine (fixed setting, fixed cast, a problem-of-the-week) over accumulating change, because accumulating change is exactly what breaks a stripped rerun package.
entries.example: Columbo (1968–2003, NBC then ABC), Law & Order (1990–2010, NBC).
entries.application: A writer designs the reset — what returns to zero by the closing credits — before designing the case or crime of the week, because the reset is the asset a rerun buyer or a stripped syndication slot is actually purchasing, not that week's particular plot.

entries.name: The Serial
entries.description: A series whose episodes accumulate change that does not reset, so watching out of order breaks comprehension.
entries.principle: Serial form trades the episodic series' rerun portability for cumulative stakes, and that trade is a commissioning fact: a serial is much harder to strip into daily reruns or sell into a market expecting broadcast-order flexibility, which is why serials cluster on channels and platforms that do not depend on stripped-rerun revenue to fill a schedule.
entries.example: The Wire (2002–2008, HBO), Breaking Bad (2008–2013, AMC).
entries.application: A writer keeps a running state ledger — who knows what, who has changed, what cannot be undone — that an episodic-series writer does not need, because the commission bets on an audience that watched episode one before it watches episode ten.

entries.name: The Anthology, Series and Episode
entries.description: A programme that renews its cast and setting, and sometimes its whole format, each episode or season under one recurring title.
entries.principle: The anthology decouples the writer's unit of labour from the show's unit of continuity: each episode (or each season, in a season-anthology) is a self-contained commission inside a recurring package, which is what let The Twilight Zone survive changing its own runtime mid-run without breaking any internal continuity a continuing series would have had to protect.
entries.example: The Twilight Zone (1959–1964, CBS), Black Mirror (2011– , Channel 4 then Netflix), American Horror Story (2011– , FX).
entries.application: A writer treats the frame — host, title sequence, house tone — as the only continuity obligation, and is licensed to change genre, cast and even episode length from one instalment to the next, a freedom a continuing series' writer does not have because that show is commissioned around a cast, not a slot.

entries.name: The Limited Series
entries.description: A serial produced to a fixed, announced ending — a closed order rather than a continuing one.
entries.principle: Where a returning series' writer must protect the possibility of renewal, a limited series is commissioned to end, so the writer can plot toward an actual conclusion from the first script rather than managing the ending as a contingency that may be deferred by a network decision.
entries.example: Chernobyl (2019, HBO, five episodes), The Night Of (2016, HBO, eight episodes).
entries.application: A writer breaks the final scene in the room in week one, because there is no later renewal decision that could force a different ending than the one the order was sold on.

entries.name: The Continuing Drama — Soap and Telenovela
entries.description: Two open-cast continuing dramas that differ in one commissioning fact: the soap is ordered indefinitely, the telenovela is ordered to a fixed close set before the first episode airs.
entries.principle: A soap is renewed strip by strip with no announced ending built into the commission, so its writers plot as though the show might run for decades. A telenovela's broadcaster sets its total run — commonly numbering in the low hundreds of episodes — before production starts, so its writers plot the whole arc, including the ending, from the outset, the way a limited series does, but at many times the length.
entries.example: Coronation Street (1960– , ITV), Avenida Brasil (2012, Rede Globo, 179 episodes).
entries.application: A telenovela writer plots toward a specific, dated finale from episode one; a soap writer designs every storyline to be extendable or cuttable on short notice, because the soap's commission never promises an ending to write toward.

entries.name: The Sketch and Variety Unit
entries.description: A show built from self-contained sketches or acts under one recurring host and slot, rather than a continuing story.
entries.principle: The unit of commission is the segment, not the episode's plot: each week's writing staff assembles a set from a pool of stand-alone premises, so what is renewed is format continuity — host, house band, desk — not narrative continuity, which lets the show survive complete turnover of cast, writers and tone from one broadcast to the next.
entries.example: Saturday Night Live (1975– , NBC), The Two Ronnies (1971–1987, BBC).
entries.application: A writer pitches and breaks an individual sketch to compete for one of a fixed number of slots in a single broadcast hour, rather than developing a throughline across the episode — the writing unit is the five-minute premise, not the show.

entries.name: The Single Play and the Television Film
entries.description: A one-off dramatic work commissioned and produced for a single transmission, with no episode structure at all.
entries.principle: The single play is the form where television commissioning most resembles theatre or film production — one script, one shoot, one broadcast date — and its retreat from network schedules is itself a commissioning-history fact: the BBC's Play for Today strand, which had commissioned one single drama a week since 1970, was axed in 1984, and ITV's rival strand Armchair Theatre wound down over the same decade.
entries.example: Cathy Come Home (1966, BBC, The Wednesday Play), Duel (1971, ABC television film).
entries.application: A writer working to a single-transmission commission is freed from every continuing-series obligation — no bible to maintain, no cast contract to protect across seasons, no act-break grid to hit week after week — and instead writes to the constraints of one runtime and one broadcast date only.

entries.name: The Pilot and the Backdoor Pilot
entries.description: A single trial episode commissioned to test a series before a full order — or, as a backdoor pilot, an episode of an existing show that doubles as the trial for a spin-off.
entries.principle: A pilot is written to sell twice, to the network deciding whether to order a series and to the audience deciding whether to return, and a backdoor pilot carries a third obligation on top: it must satisfy the parent show's own episode and audience, who did not sign up to watch an advertisement for a different series.
entries.example: Lost (2004, ABC, stand-alone pilot), "My Favorite Orkan" (1978, Happy Days, ABC — the backdoor pilot for Mork & Mindy).
entries.application: A writer of a backdoor pilot has to seed a full cast and premise inside the space a parent series can spare from its own episode's function, so the new material must resolve as a satisfying beat of the show the regular audience already watches, not only as a trailer for the one that does not exist yet.

entries.name: The Short Order
entries.description: A continuing season commissioned to fewer episodes than a traditional full network season — commonly six to thirteen — without the fixed, announced ending of a limited series.
entries.principle: A short order is a distinct commissioning category from both the pilot and the limited series: it is a continuing series that may or may not be renewed, simply ordered thin, which forces a different arithmetic on how much story to spend per episode when the writer does not know whether a second order will exist to spend the rest on.
entries.example: True Detective (2014– , HBO, eight episodes per season), Fleabag (2016–2019, BBC Three, six episodes per season).
entries.application: A writer on a short order compresses the mid-season complications that a 22-episode network season can spread across filler weeks, because there is no slack in the order to spend on a stand-alone episode that does not move the season's spine.

entries.name: The Network Season
entries.description: The traditional US broadcast-network commission — historically around twenty-two episodes ordered against a September-to-May schedule.
entries.principle: The network season's episode count is set by the advertising calendar — filling a year-round schedule and hitting the Nielsen ratings sweeps periods (November, February, May) that set the ad rates a network can charge — rather than by story need, and that is the commissioning fact behind the "bottle episode" and the clip show: a season long enough to need filler weeks that a short order never has.
entries.example: Grey's Anatomy (2005– , ABC), The Office (2005–2013, NBC).
entries.application: A writer on a network season budgets two or three flexible episodes that can be produced cheaply or reordered without damaging the arc, because the order is long enough that not every episode can be load-bearing to the season's spine.

entries.name: The Streaming Drop
entries.description: A season commissioned for simultaneous release of every episode on one date, rather than a weekly transmission slot.
entries.principle: Removing the weekly broadcast slot removes the writer's main lever for pacing a cliffhanger against a fixed re-attendance date a week later; the drop replaces "make them come back next week" with "make them not stop now," which collapses the season's internal shape closer to one long film than to a broadcast series.
entries.example: House of Cards (2013, Netflix, first full-season same-day release), Stranger Things (2016– , Netflix).
entries.application: A writer on a drop-commissioned season times cliffhangers to a binge session's natural pause points rather than to a seven-day gap, and can drop the "previously on" recap a weekly slot requires but a same-sitting viewer does not need.

entries.name: The Returning Series and the Renewal
entries.description: A series commissioned season by season, whose continuation past its current order is a business decision made outside the writers' room, usually after the season is already written.
entries.principle: The renewal decision is the single commissioning fact that most shapes a continuing series' plotting — a writer protects the show's ability to keep running (no death that forecloses a needed story option, no ending that only works if renewal is declined) because the decision to continue is not the writers' to make and is frequently not known until after the season is shot.
entries.example: Supernatural (2005–2020, The CW), The Good Place (2016–2020, NBC).
entries.application: A writer plots a season finale as a fork — satisfying if the show is renewed, closeable if it is not — because the renewal decision typically arrives after the season the writer is currently plotting has already been written.

entries.name: The Revival, the Reboot and the Continuation
entries.description: A series recommissioned after cancellation or a long gap — as a continuation with the same cast and continuity, a reboot with a new cast or continuity on the same premise, or a fixed-run revival.
entries.principle: A revival is commissioned against an audience's prior knowledge of the original run, a constraint no first-run series carries, so the writer must decide how much elapsed real time to acknowledge and whether original-cast availability — age, contract, death — forecloses storylines the original run left open.
entries.example: Twin Peaks: The Return (2017, Showtime, a quarter-century after the original series' 1991 cancellation), Fuller House (2016–2020, Netflix, continuation of Full House).
entries.application: A writer on a revival spends the audience's memory of the original deliberately — callbacks, aged-up characters, the visible gap itself — as material, rather than routing around it, because the commission exists specifically because that memory is marketable.

entries.name: The Quiz and Game Show
entries.description: A non-scripted format built around contestants answering questions or completing tasks for a prize, produced to a strict, repeatable segment structure rather than a written script.
entries.principle: A quiz show's writing lives almost entirely in the paper format — the round structure, the scoring, the jeopardy mechanism — because the actual broadcast content, contestants' answers, cannot be scripted at all; the format document, not a teleplay, is the object that gets commissioned and later licensed abroad.
entries.example: Jeopardy! (1964–1975 daytime, NBC; syndicated since 1984), Countdown (1982– , Channel 4).
entries.application: A format writer writes rules robust enough to survive any contestant's behaviour — tie-break procedures, timing, disqualification triggers — because unlike a scripted cast, the people on screen are unrehearsed and the format must not be able to break live on air.

entries.name: The Panel Show
entries.description: A non-scripted format built around a host and a rotating or regular panel of guests responding, unscripted, to prepared prompts.
entries.principle: A panel show is written almost entirely as prompts and pre-researched material handed to a host and panellists who then respond unscripted on air, so the craft skill is engineering a question that is answerable in an entertaining way — a line a panellist gets to, rather than a line written to be delivered verbatim, which is the seam against a sitcom's scripted joke.
entries.example: Have I Got News for You (1990– , BBC), QI (2003– , BBC).
entries.application: A writer supplies the host with researched material and possible lines of attack rather than dialogue, and structures the segment so a panellist's own unscripted response fills the runtime — the delivered product is a briefing document, not a script.

entries.name: The Reality Competition
entries.description: A non-scripted format that places contestants in a structured competitive environment across a fixed elimination arc, ending in a single winner.
entries.principle: The season's commissioned episode order fixes the elimination arithmetic before a single frame is shot — an order of N episodes with one elimination a week requires a specific number of contestants at the start — so the non-scripted story team's job is to build a season-long elimination schedule to fit a length the network set in advance.
entries.example: Survivor (2000– , CBS), The Great British Bake Off (2010– , BBC then Channel 4).
entries.application: A story producer works the elimination arc's arithmetic backward from the commissioned episode count — how many contestants must start, how many must leave each week — before casting even begins, because the order length is fixed before the show exists to shoot around it.

entries.name: Structured Reality and the Constructed Documentary
entries.description: A non-scripted format that follows real, often self-cast people through situations engineered by producers, without a competitive elimination structure.
entries.principle: The commissioning distinction from documentary proper is the degree of producer-engineered situation: a structured-reality format is ordered to a season and episode count like a scripted show, and a non-scripted story room breaks that season into planted storylines and confrontations timed to episode length, even though no line of dialogue is scripted in advance.
entries.example: The Hills (2006–2010, MTV), The Only Way Is Essex (2010– , ITV2).
entries.application: A story producer breaks a season the way a scripted room breaks story — beats, act breaks, a season arc — but achieves each beat by scheduling real people into engineered situations and assembling the result afterward in the edit, rather than by writing lines in advance.

entries.name: The Talent Search
entries.description: A non-scripted format that auditions members of the public for a prize, typically a recording or performing contract, across an elimination arc combining performance with an audience or judge vote.
entries.principle: The talent search's defining commissioning fact against the general reality competition is the vote mechanism: because a public phone or app vote — not a producer-run panel alone — determines who survives, the format's writing is chiefly in the rule for combining vote and judge input, and that rule is the core intellectual property licensed when the format is sold into a new territory.
entries.example: Pop Idol (2001–2003, ITV), American Idol (2002– , Fox then ABC).
entries.application: A format writer specifies the exact arithmetic of vote-plus-judge combination — proportion, tie-break, any save mechanism — as the primary deliverable, because that rule, not the audition footage, is what a licensee abroad is actually buying.

entries.name: The Makeover and Transformation Format
entries.description: A non-scripted format built around the before-and-after transformation of a person, home or object, hosted by expert specialists, within a fixed single-episode or short-arc structure.
entries.principle: The makeover format's commissioning unit is usually the episode rather than the season: each instalment is a self-contained transformation with its own budget and expert team, closer in structure to the episodic series than to the reality competition's season-long elimination math, which is why makeover formats survive being stripped into daily or twice-weekly slots.
entries.example: Queer Eye (2003–2007, Bravo; revived 2018– , Netflix), Extreme Makeover: Home Edition (2003–2012, ABC).
entries.application: A writer or producer designs each episode to resolve completely — reveal, reaction, credits — rather than serialising the transformation across a season, because the format is commissioned and scheduled like the episodic series, not built to hold an audience across a week's gap.

entries.name: The Dating Format
entries.description: A non-scripted format that structures romantic pairing between contestants as a competitive, elimination-driven process across a commissioned season order.
entries.principle: The dating format borrows the reality competition's elimination arc, but its prize is a relationship rather than a cash sum or a contract, which pushes the format toward manufactured decision points — a rose ceremony, a recoupling — timed to fixed calendar intervals rather than to courtship's own pace; the format imposes an elimination schedule on the romance, not the reverse.
entries.example: The Bachelor (2002– , ABC), Love Island (2015– , ITV2).
entries.application: A story producer schedules artificial decision ceremonies at fixed episode intervals to manufacture elimination beats on a courtship that has no natural elimination rhythm of its own, borrowing the season order's arithmetic from the reality competition rather than from any real dating timeline.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Procedural
entries.description: A scripted genre built around a case, patient or investigation resolved within each episode, commissioned to run open-ended across however many seasons a network renews.
entries.principle: The procedural's case-of-the-week engine is a direct commissioning answer, not a content preference: it lets a single hour satisfy both a network season's need for roughly twenty-two episodes a year and a syndication market that requires episodes to be watchable in any order once resold.
entries.example: Dragnet (1951–1959, NBC), CSI: Crime Scene Investigation (2000–2015, CBS).
entries.application: A writer keeps any season-long serialized subplot separable from the case-of-the-week spine, so an episode can be cut, reordered or resold without damaging the self-contained case a rerun buyer is actually purchasing.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Prestige Serial
entries.description: A scripted serial commissioned to a short, expensively produced order, typically on subscription cable or a streaming platform, trading the network season's episode count for cost and creative latitude per episode.
entries.principle: The prestige serial inverts the network season's arithmetic — fewer episodes, more expensive each, financed by subscription rather than advertising — which is what frees the writer to plot a single sustained arc a stripped-rerun, ad-supported economy could not carry.
entries.example: The Sopranos (1999–2007, HBO), Mad Men (2007–2015, AMC).
entries.application: A writer plots one continuous throughline across the entire ordered run rather than budgeting reorderable "flex" episodes, because the commission's financing model rewards density over the repeatability a longer, ad-funded season would require.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Multi-Camera Sitcom
entries.description: A sitcom shot with several cameras before a studio audience, edited from simultaneous coverage — a production form the commission fixes, not a joke style.
entries.principle: The multi-camera commission ties act structure to what a studio audience's real laughter can carry in one continuous take across a small number of standing sets, typically shot in a single studio day, which sets a hard ceiling on how many locations or costume changes a script can call for.
entries.example: Cheers (1982–1993, NBC), The Big Bang Theory (2007–2019, CBS).
entries.application: A writer scripts scenes long enough to build to a laugh a live studio audience can actually deliver in real time, and confines the story to sets the standing stage can hold, rather than writing for coverage assembled later from many separate locations.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Single-Camera Sitcom
entries.description: A sitcom shot with one camera and no studio audience, using film-style production technique — a production form the commission fixes, not a joke style.
entries.principle: Removing the studio audience removes the multi-camera form's built-in laugh-timing constraint, which frees the single-camera commission to shoot on location, cut at any pace, and build jokes around a visual cut or a to-camera aside rather than a scene playing out in real time for a room to react to.
entries.example: Arrested Development (2003–2006, Fox; revived 2013–2019, Netflix), The Office (2005–2013, NBC).
entries.application: A writer scripts for the edit — cutaways, mockumentary-style asides, coverage assembled from multiple takes and locations — because there is no studio audience's real-time laugh to protect or pace against.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Soap Opera
entries.description: A continuing drama produced and transmitted on a near-daily or multi-weekly strip schedule, which is the commissioning fact that most separates its writing process from any other continuing drama.
entries.principle: A soap's script-to-air turnaround is measured in days, so no single writer can hold the whole story: the commission requires a team of parallel writers working weeks or months ahead of transmission under one story editor and a shared bible, a production discipline a once-weekly drama does not need.
entries.example: Coronation Street (1960– , ITV), General Hospital (1963– , ABC).
entries.application: A writer works from a story editor's detailed breakdown rather than originating an episode's plot alone, because the strip schedule's turnaround speed requires many scripts to be in simultaneous progress under one continuity authority.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Teen Series
entries.description: A scripted series commissioned for and marketed to a teenage demographic, historically scheduled around a network's youth-targeted block or a network built specifically for that audience.
entries.principle: The teen series' commissioning fact is the demographic remit of its slot or network — The CW was built explicitly to reach the young audience advertisers pay a premium for — and that remit sets constraints a general drama slot does not: content limits, an ensemble young enough to plausibly recast across a multi-year renewal, and storylines timed to a school-year calendar.
entries.example: Beverly Hills, 90210 (1990–2000, Fox), Riverdale (2017–2023, The CW).
entries.application: A writer paces season arcs against an in-universe school year and budgets for cast turnover as actors age out of the premise, because the commission's demographic remit, not the story, sets the show's natural cast lifespan.

entries.category: Scripted Genres as Television Commissions Them
entries.name: The Children's Series and the Broadcast Remit
entries.description: A series commissioned specifically for a children's-hours slot or channel, governed by content and scheduling rules a general-audience commission does not carry.
entries.principle: A UK children's commission is bound by remit-specific regulation before a line of dialogue is drafted — Ofcom's Broadcasting Code sets stricter content standards for programmes made for or scheduled around children, and the BBC's public remit carries a dedicated children's-output requirement — which is a commissioning constraint, not a house-style preference.
entries.example: Grange Hill (1978–2008, BBC), Sesame Street (1969– , PBS then HBO/Max).
entries.application: A writer checks a scene against the remit's content rules before drafting it, not after, because the commission itself, not house style, sets the hard limits on violence, language and theme.

entries.name: The Commercial Network and the Ad Break
entries.description: A network financed by selling advertising time within the programme, which fixes the show's internal act structure to the number and placement of commercial breaks the schedule sells.
entries.principle: The ad break is written into the script as a commissioning fact, not inserted afterward: a US commercial-network hour is built to four or five act breaks, each written to end on a hook strong enough to survive a two-to-three-minute interruption, a structural requirement a public-service or ad-free platform commission does not impose.
entries.example: 24 (2001–2010, Fox), Desperate Housewives (2004–2012, ABC).
entries.application: A writer plots each act to land its hook exactly at the ad-break mark rather than distributing tension evenly across the hour, because the network sells that specific interruption point to advertisers and the script must justify the audience returning after it.

entries.name: The Licensed Format Remake
entries.description: A scripted or non-scripted series produced in one territory under license from a format first devised and produced in another, built from a format bible rather than an original premise.
entries.principle: A licensed remake's commissioning fact is the format bible itself — a paper document specifying structure, rules and sometimes shot-by-shot direction — so the licensing territory's writers adapt within a locked structure rather than inventing one, and the license contract, not the writer, sets what may and may not change before a page is written.
entries.example: The Office (2005–2013, NBC, US remake of the UK's The Office), Ugly Betty (2006–2010, ABC, US remake of Colombia's Yo soy Betty, la fea).
entries.application: A writer on a licensed remake works from the format bible to decide what to localise — references, casting, running time — and what the license requires to stay fixed, rather than starting the premise from a blank page.

entries.name: The Tokusatsu Line and the Japanese Broadcast Serial
entries.description: A Japanese-originated line of live-action special-effects series commissioned to a distinct broadcast rhythm and merchandising cycle largely absent from Western television commissioning.
entries.principle: A tokusatsu series is commissioned around an annual or near-annual full-cast replacement — a new costumed hero, a new cast, a new toy line launching with the new broadcast year — a discipline closer to a fashion-season product cycle than to a Western returning series' renewal logic, where the same cast and costume are the asset being protected.
entries.example: 仮面ライダー / Kamen Rider (1971 tv), ウルトラン / Ultraman (1966 tv).
entries.application: A writer on a tokusatsu commission designs a season that ends completely, with no cast, costume or continuity expected to carry into next year's series, rather than protecting continuity for renewal, because the commercial logic renews the toy line, not the cast.

entries.name: The Co-Production
entries.description: A series commissioned and financed jointly by broadcasters or producers in two or more territories, sharing budget and creative control under a co-production agreement.
entries.principle: A co-production's commissioning fact is a split financing and delivery obligation — each partner territory typically requires a minimum quota of its own cast, crew or filming days for the show to qualify as a domestic production under its own subsidy or quota rules — a constraint a single-territory commission never carries.
entries.example: Bron/Broen (2011–2018, SVT Sweden and DR Denmark), The Tunnel (2013–2018, Sky Atlantic UK and Canal+ France).
entries.application: A writer on a co-production casts and locates storylines to satisfy each partner's minimum domestic-content requirement — a cast split roughly by territory, plots that cross the shared border — because the financing itself, not the story, requires each partner's contribution to be visible on screen.

entries.name: The Sitcom's Joke Engine
entries.description: The sitcom's joke, its runner and its reaction signal, as Comedy reads them; this pack cards only the two production forms — multi-camera and single-camera — the sitcom is commissioned in.
entries.principle: Measured against Comedy's own register, "showrunner" appears zero times and there is no card on the act break, the pilot, the order, the slot, the bible, the season arc, the renewal or the format sale — Comedy owns the joke entirely, and nothing in the commission changes what makes a line funny. This subject is handed off to the `comedy-reference` pack.
entries.example: Fawlty Towers (1975–1979, BBC), Frasier (1993–2004, NBC).
entries.application: A writer working the joke itself — the setup, the runner, the callback — should consult Comedy's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about camera configuration and season order, covered under The Multi-Camera Sitcom and The Single-Camera Sitcom.

entries.name: The Serialised Comic and Its Screen Line
entries.description: The manga's own print serialisation — survey feedback, the weekly magazine, the uncredited editor, the ten-week cancellation horizon — as Manga cards it; this pack cards only its television broadcast descendants.
entries.principle: Manga cards print serialisation in full and declined the entire television tokusatsu line to this pack with stated reasons; the page-to-panel craft of magazine serialisation does not change when a story moves to broadcast, so that craft stays Manga's. This subject is handed off to the `manga-reference` pack.
entries.example: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball (1984–1995, Weekly Shōnen Jump), 仮面ライダー / Kamen Rider (1971 tv).
entries.application: A writer working the print serial's survey-driven, chapter-by-chapter craft should consult Manga's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about the broadcast serial's episode order and merchandising cycle, covered under The Tokusatsu Line and the Japanese Broadcast Serial.

entries.name: The Costumed Hero on Television
entries.description: The costumed hero's mandate, costume and continuity, as Superhero reads them; this pack cards only the commissioning shape — the season order, the network mandate as a rights device — that houses the character.
entries.principle: Superhero already cards eighteen tv-medium entries, roughly twelve of them functionally format cards, and holds its own ten-card block on the mandate and the trade — the genuine overlap this pack shares with Superhero, resolved by: we card the commission, Superhero cards the mandate. This subject is handed off to the `superhero-reference` pack.
entries.example: The Adventures of Superman (1952–1958, syndicated), Daredevil (2015–2018, Netflix).
entries.application: A writer working the hero's mandate, costume rules or continuity should consult Superhero's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about the season's episode order and renewal, covered under The Returning Series and the Renewal.

entries.name: Screen Science Fiction
entries.description: The idea, the novum and the extrapolation as Science Fiction reads them; this pack cards only the anthology as a commissioned form, a territory SF's own reading leaves vacant.
entries.principle: Science Fiction cards The Twilight Zone and Black Mirror as containers for its own short form but cards no anthology form entry at all — no subgenre, craft, trope or checklist card on the form itself — so this pack cards the anthology's commissioning shape (per-episode budget independence, the host as a rights device) while leaving the speculative idea to SF. This subject is handed off to the `sf-reference` pack.
entries.example: The Twilight Zone (1959–1964, CBS), Black Mirror (2011– , Channel 4 then Netflix).
entries.application: A writer working the speculative idea or the novum should consult SF's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about anthology commissioning, covered under The Anthology, Series and Episode.

entries.name: The Horror Series and Its Weekly Dread
entries.description: Dread, revulsion and the body as Horror reads them; this pack cards only the commissioning shape of the horror series' seasonal or anthology structure.
entries.principle: What makes a scene frightening does not change when the episode order changes, so the affect itself stays Horror's; only the container — season length, anthology reset, the streaming drop's binge pacing — is this pack's to card. This subject is handed off to the `horror-reference` pack.
entries.example: American Horror Story (2011– , FX), The Haunting of Hill House (2018, Netflix).
entries.application: A writer working dread, revulsion or the scare itself should consult Horror's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about season-anthology structure, covered under The Anthology, Series and Episode.

entries.name: The Crime Procedural's Puzzle
entries.description: The puzzle, the clue and the fair-play contract with the audience as Mystery-Crime-Thriller reads them; this pack cards only the commissioning shape that houses the puzzle.
entries.principle: Whether a clue is fairly planted does not change when the order length changes, so the puzzle's own craft stays Mystery-Crime-Thriller's; this pack cards only why the case-of-the-week structure exists as a commissioning answer to the network season's length and the syndication market's need for order-independence. This subject is handed off to the `mystery-crime-thriller-reference` pack.
entries.example: Columbo (1968–2003, NBC then ABC), Broadchurch (2013–2017, ITV).
entries.application: A writer working the clue's fair-play placement or the puzzle's construction should consult Mystery-Crime-Thriller's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about the procedural's commissioning shape, covered under The Procedural.

entries.name: The Courtship Promise as a Genre Contract
entries.description: The courtship promise as a genre object — the will-they-won't-they contract with the audience — as Romance reads it; this pack keeps only the commissioning fact that changes it in a continuing drama.
entries.principle: Narrowed from an earlier draft that handed off the continuing drama's romance wholesale — wrong, because under this pack's own boundary rule the renewal decision is the courtship structure in a continuing drama: renewal keeps a couple in orbit, cancellation forces the promise to resolve early. What transfers is the promise as a genre contract, not its commissioning. This subject is handed off to the `romance-reference` pack.
entries.example: Moonlighting (1985–1989, ABC), Bridgerton (2020– , Netflix).
entries.application: A writer working the courtship promise's own genre grammar — what a "will-they" contract obligates a writer to pay off — should consult Romance's craft cards, not this pack's; here, the decisions are about how renewal or cancellation forces that payoff's timing, covered under The Returning Series and the Renewal and The Continuing Drama — Soap and Telenovela.

entries.name: The Public-Service Remit
entries.description: A broadcaster funded wholly or partly against a defined public-service obligation rather than solely against advertising or subscription, which changes what a writer is commissioned to make and for whom.
entries.principle: A public-service remit is a commissioning instrument before it is a political position: it obliges a broadcaster to criteria a purely commercial platform does not carry — universal reach, originating-content quotas, an inform-educate-entertain mandate — and those criteria are enforced by a named instrument, the BBC's Royal Charter and licence fee being the clearest case and by no means the only shape. The writer's practical position under such a remit differs from the commercial one in a specific way: a premise can be commissioned because it serves an obligation nobody expects to be profitable, and a premise can be refused on remit grounds a commercial network would never apply. Whether that obligation is a public good that its funding mechanism is the price of, or a subsidy that distorts the market it competes in, is argued in every territory that has one and is argued by serious people on both sides.
entries.example: Blue Planet II (2017, BBC One) was commissioned against a natural-history obligation older than any ratings case for it; PBS NewsHour (1975–, PBS) runs an hour of news nightly on a funding model no advertising-funded schedule has sustained.
entries.application: Before pitching to a public-service broadcaster, find the specific public-purpose test in its charter or remit and write the pitch's one-paragraph answer to it, because that answer is a commissioning criterion and not a courtesy — and hold the same premise up against a commercial network's revenue test, because the two will accept and refuse different things about it.

entries.name: The Closed-Ended Serial as an Export
entries.description: A serial commissioned to a fixed length ends, and a story that ends can be sold complete to a broadcaster that did not commission it — which is a constraint on how it is written, not only on how it is sold.
entries.principle: The commissioning decision that fixes a serial's total run before production also makes it exportable, because a buyer in another territory can acquire a finished, countable object with an ending rather than an open commitment to a programme that may run for decades. That saleability reaches back into the writing: a serial built for export is written so its arc survives dubbing and subtitling, so its episode count fits a foreign schedule's strip, and so its resolution does not depend on knowledge a viewer outside the originating territory cannot have. The Latin American industries built the clearest version of this, and the reading of what that export record represents is itself contested — one account treats it as a major non-Anglophone cultural export that reversed the usual direction of trade, another as evidence that what travels is the structure while the specificity of origin is what gets dubbed away — and this card carries the tension rather than settling it.
entries.example: Yo soy Betty, la fea (1999–2001, RCN Televisión, Colombia) closed at a fixed length and was subsequently licensed into dozens of territories; Avenida Brasil (2012, Rede Globo) was built to a fixed close and sold widely on the strength of having one.
entries.application: If a serial may be sold outside the territory that commissioned it, audit every plot turn that depends on local knowledge — an institution, a public figure, a legal procedure — and decide deliberately whether to keep it as texture the export buyer will accept or to carry the information inside the scene; and place the arc's resolution where a fixed episode count guarantees it, not where a renewal might have allowed it.

entries.name: The Cold Open as Contract
entries.description: The pre-title sequence promises the audience what kind of hour they bought before the theme song confirms it.
entries.principle: Open on the show's genre engine turning, not on set-up — the cold open sells the format, not the plot.
entries.example: The Simpsons (1989– , Fox) opens on a self-contained sight gag most weeks, disconnected from that episode's plot; Law & Order (1990–2010, NBC) opens on the discovery of the body that starts the case.
entries.application: A writer drafts the cold open last, after the episode's engine is known, so it can advertise that specific engine rather than stall for time before the story starts.

entries.name: Internal Resolution Inside Arc Television
entries.description: Even a serialized drama closes something by the credits, so a single episode still reads as a unit and not just a fragment.
entries.principle: Give every episode its own small close even inside a season-long arc — the arc plot may continue, but something has to land tonight.
entries.example: Breaking Bad (2008–2013, AMC) closes most hours on a scene-level resolution — a decision made, a body disposed of — while the season arc keeps running underneath.
entries.application: A writer identifies the episode's own question in the outline stage, separate from the season's question, and makes sure it gets answered by the act-out.

entries.name: The Act-Out as Hook, Not Summary
entries.description: The line or image before a commercial break has one job — get the viewer to sit through the break — and summarizing what just happened is not that job.
entries.principle: End an act on a question, a reveal or a threat, never on a recap of what the act already told the audience.
entries.example: The X-Files (1993–2002, Fox) built entire mid-season episodes around act-out reveals timed to the network's break grid.
entries.application: A writer reads the last line of every act out loud and asks whether a viewer with a remote in hand has a reason to stay; if the answer is only curiosity about the plot so far, the act-out is rewritten.

entries.name: The Clip Show as Production Economics
entries.description: An episode built from flashback footage to previously aired scenes, commissioned to save a production week's budget, not to serve the story.
entries.principle: Treat a clip show as a budget instrument first and a story opportunity second — the constraint came before the premise.
entries.example: Roseanne (1988–1997, ABC) and Cheers (1982–1993, NBC) both produced clip episodes framed as a character's memory to justify the reused footage.
entries.application: A writer given a clip-show order finds the one piece of new material — a frame story, a single new scene — that makes the reused footage feel chosen rather than recycled.

entries.name: The Premise as a Repeating Engine
entries.description: A commissioned series states its premise once and then has to generate a new episode from the identical machine every week for years.
entries.principle: Design the format so the premise regenerates a fresh problem on its own, without the writer having to invent a new engine each week.
entries.example: House (2004–2012, Fox) generates its weekly episode from one fixed engine — a diagnostic mystery — that does not need reinventing case to case.
entries.application: A writer pressure-tests a pitch by asking whether it can produce twenty-two different problems from the same premise without repeating itself; if it can only produce three, the premise is a story, not a format.

entries.name: The Special or Event Episode's Different Job
entries.description: A clip show's opposite — an episode built to depart from the show's normal engine for one week, announced to the audience as an event.
entries.principle: An event episode is allowed to break the show's own rules for one week precisely because it is marked as a departure, not the new normal.
entries.example: Community (2009–2015, NBC then Yahoo! Screen) regularly produced format-departure episodes — a bottle-episode courtroom drama, a stop-motion Christmas special — inside a sitcom otherwise built on a fixed engine.
entries.application: A writer of an event episode states in the room, before breaking story, exactly which rule is being suspended for the week and confirms the following episode restores it.

entries.name: The Cold Open's Length Is Set by the Break Grid
entries.description: How long a show can run before its first commercial break is a scheduling fact handed to the writer, not a creative choice.
entries.principle: Learn the network's act-break grid before drafting the cold open — the runtime to the first break is a spec, not a preference.
entries.example: A US network hour drama's cold open is commonly built to run under five minutes before the first break; a premium-cable or streaming drama with no ad grid can run a cold open considerably longer.
entries.application: A writer confirms the commissioning platform's break grid at the outset of a pilot script, because a cold open timed for broadcast's ad structure and one timed for an ad-free platform are different pieces of writing.

entries.name: The Previously On as Serial Memory Device
entries.description: The recap segment that opens a serialized episode, restating only what this week's story needs the audience to remember.
entries.principle: A Previously On segment is authored, not assembled — it is written to make one specific fact land for this week's plot, not to summarize the season.
entries.example: Lost (2004–2010, ABC) used its Previously On segment to seed a fact the audience would need minutes later, effectively pre-loading a plot beat inside the recap itself.
entries.application: A writer drafts the recap segment against the finished script, choosing clips that plant this episode's needed information rather than defaulting to what happened last time.

entries.name: The Commercial Break Writes the Act Structure
entries.description: A commercial network's ad grid determines how many acts a script has and roughly how long each one runs, before a single scene is broken.
entries.principle: Break story to the network's act count first — a four-act hour and a five-act hour are different outlines, not the same outline cut differently.
entries.example: A US broadcast-network hour drama commonly runs a four- or five-act structure set by the ad grid; a UK single-drama slot on the BBC, carrying no mid-programme advertising, is not built to the same grid.
entries.application: A writer confirms the commissioning network's act count in the outline stage, because moving an act break after the room has broken story to the wrong number costs a rewrite, not an edit.

entries.name: The Teaser and Tag as Bookends Outside the Act Count
entries.description: The cold open and the closing tag sit outside the numbered acts, carrying no act-break obligation of their own.
entries.principle: Write the teaser and tag as bookends that frame the numbered acts, not as an extra act competing for the same real estate.
entries.example: Many US procedural dramas run a teaser before Act One and a short tag after the final act, both explicitly excluded from the act count that governs the ad breaks.
entries.application: A writer keeps the tag short and detached from the episode's driving plot, since its job is a closing beat, not a fifth act carrying unresolved story weight.

entries.name: The Act-Out Cliffhanger vs the Soft Act-Out
entries.description: Two different tools for ending an act — a hard cliffhanger built to force a return, and a softer button that closes a beat without threatening the audience.
entries.principle: Reserve the hard cliffhanger for the acts that most need to survive a channel change, and let interior acts close on a softer button.
entries.example: 24 (2001–2010, Fox) built almost every act-out as a hard cliffhanger timed to its real-time structure; a multi-camera sitcom more often closes an interior act on a soft joke button instead.
entries.application: A writer varies act-out intensity across an episode deliberately, because five hard cliffhangers in one hour numb the device the same way five hard cliffhangers in one season do.

entries.name: The Streaming Break-less Act Still Keeps Act Shape
entries.description: A platform with no mid-episode advertising removes the commercial break but does not remove the underlying act structure a writer breaks story to.
entries.principle: Keep writing to act turns even without a break to write toward — the turn is a story tool, not just an ad-placement marker.
entries.example: House of Cards (2013–2018, Netflix) carried no mid-episode ad breaks, yet was scripted by television veterans who retained internal act markers inherited from broadcast-drama craft.
entries.application: A writer on an ad-free platform still marks act turns in the outline, because removing the turn along with the break tends to produce an episode that drifts rather than one that simply flows.

entries.name: The British Half-Hour's Unbroken Act
entries.description: A UK single-channel comedy or drama slot without a mid-programme commercial break is written as one continuous movement rather than a sequence of act-outs.
entries.principle: Do not import a US-style act-out rhythm into a slot that carries no break to write toward.
entries.example: Fawlty Towers (1975–1979, BBC) runs its half hour as one unbroken build with no act-out beats, unlike a US multi-camera sitcom scripted around three commercial breaks.
entries.application: A writer commissioned for an unbroken slot builds escalation continuously across the runtime instead of resetting tension at act markers borrowed from a broadcast-with-ads tradition.

entries.name: The Multi-Camera Sitcom's Live-Audience Rhythm
entries.description: A multi-camera sitcom's act structure is built around where the studio audience needs a reset, not only where the ad break falls.
entries.principle: Build act breaks at points where a live audience's attention can be reset by a scene or set change, since the studio taping schedule depends on it.
entries.example: Cheers (1982–1993, NBC) structured its acts around bar-set scenes that allowed set and costume resets between filmed segments in front of a live audience.
entries.application: A writer on a multi-camera show times act breaks to production reset points as much as to story turns, because the studio floor, not only the story, has to be able to use the break.

entries.name: The Case-of-the-Week Act Turn
entries.description: A procedural's act breaks are conventionally built around escalating investigative reveals rather than emotional turns.
entries.principle: Turn a procedural act on a new piece of evidence or a wrong suspect cleared, not on a character beat alone.
entries.example: Law & Order (1990–2010, NBC) structures its acts around investigative escalation — a witness, a suspect, a twist in evidence — with character material kept subordinate to the case's turn.
entries.application: A writer breaking a procedural episode identifies the case-fact that turns each act before deciding which character carries the scene that reveals it.

entries.name: The Season Finale as the Largest Act-Out
entries.description: A season finale's final scene functions as an act-out at the scale of the whole season, not just the episode.
entries.principle: Write a season finale's last beat to answer the season's driving question or to reopen it, because a finale that merely resolves the week's plot wastes the position.
entries.example: The Sopranos (1999–2007, HBO) closed multiple seasons on a beat pitched at the scale of the whole run rather than the episode alone.
entries.application: A writer breaking a finale checks the season's opening question against the finale's closing image before locking either.

entries.name: The Writers' Room as Manufacturing Floor
entries.description: A staffed writers' room is organized to produce a season's worth of scripts on a schedule, which shapes how story gets broken as much as any craft principle does.
entries.principle: Treat the room's job as manufacturing episodes to a deadline, and treat any craft method that cannot survive that deadline as a method to abandon.
entries.example: The staffed-room model used across US network and cable dramas exists specifically to produce twenty-plus scripts a season on a fixed calendar, a throughput a single writer working alone cannot match.
entries.application: A showrunner designs the room's weekly rhythm — outline days, draft days, rewrite days — around the season's delivery schedule before assigning a single episode.

entries.name: The Board as Externalized Memory
entries.description: The physical or digital corkboard tracking story beats exists because no room can hold an entire season's plotting in memory across months of work.
entries.principle: Put every plotted beat on the board the day it is broken — an un-carded beat is a beat the room will re-break by accident three weeks later.
entries.example: Breaking Bad's (2008–2013, AMC) writers' room worked from a card-covered wall tracking the season's plot, later preserved as an artifact of the show's process.
entries.application: A writer assigned to update the board treats it as the room's shared record, not a private note, because the next person to walk in has to be able to read the season's state off it cold.

entries.name: The Story-Editor Hierarchy as Function, Not Just Title
entries.description: US television writing-staff titles (staff writer, story editor, executive story editor, co-producer and upward) track function and authority in the room, not seniority in years alone.
entries.principle: Read a credited title as a statement of what that writer is trusted to do unsupervised in the room, not as a label of prestige.
entries.example: The US staff ladder — staff writer through co-executive producer — is a near-universal structure across network and cable dramas, distinct from the UK's smaller commissioned-freelancer model.
entries.application: A writer entering a US staffed room for the first time learns the room's title ladder before assuming what they are and are not empowered to rewrite unsupervised.

entries.name: Breaking Backward from the Act-Out
entries.description: A common room technique — pitch the ending of an act first, then work backward to what has to happen to earn it.
entries.principle: Pitch the act-out before pitching the scenes leading to it, so the room is building toward a known target instead of hoping one appears.
entries.example: Procedural rooms breaking a case-of-the-week routinely pitch the final reveal first, then plot backward through the clues that make it land.
entries.application: A writer stuck mid-break asks the room what the act needs to end on, then works the preceding scenes to deliver exactly that, rather than continuing to pitch scenes forward and hoping for a landing.

entries.name: The Showrunner as Final Authority
entries.description: A US-model showrunner holds final creative authority over every script the room produces, whatever the credited writer's own draft said.
entries.principle: Understand that a script credit does not mean sole authorship — the showrunner's pass is the version that airs, and every writer in the room works knowing that.
entries.example: The showrunner model, distinguishing the position from a UK-style script editor with narrower authority, is documented across the US network and cable system alike.
entries.application: A staff writer drafting a script writes toward the showrunner's stated vision for the episode rather than toward their own instinct alone, because the rewrite pass will reconcile the two regardless.

entries.name: The Freelance Script vs the Staff Script
entries.description: Some episodes are commissioned from a writer outside the regular staff, under different terms and different expectations than a staffed episode.
entries.principle: A freelance script is expected to arrive close to broadcast-ready on the outline the room already broke; a staff script is expected to be broken and drafted inside the room's own process.
entries.example: US network dramas commonly commission one or two freelance scripts a season, often from outside writers the show is scouting for future staffing.
entries.application: A freelance writer confirms exactly how much of the outline is fixed before drafting, because a freelance script rewritten from the ground up by the staff defeats the purpose of the commission.

entries.name: The Table Read as Diagnostic Instrument
entries.description: A cast read-through of a finished draft, used to surface problems a page cannot show — pacing, a flat scene, a joke that does not land out loud.
entries.principle: Run the table read to find what reading silently cannot find — hear the script before deciding it is done.
entries.example: Multi-camera sitcoms built around a live studio audience, such as Friends (1994–2004, NBC), used the table read as a formal gate a script had to pass before a rewrite pass and a live taping.
entries.application: A writer treats table-read silence on a joke as data, not bad luck, and rewrites the joke rather than defending it.

entries.name: Breaking the Season Before the Episode
entries.description: A serialized show's room typically maps the season's arc in broad strokes before any single episode is broken in detail.
entries.principle: Fix the season's shape first, then break individual episodes against it — breaking episode one in detail before the season is mapped risks writing toward an ending the room has not yet chosen.
entries.example: The Wire's (2002–2008, HBO) writers' room mapped each season's institutional arc before breaking individual episodes, working from a season-long outline before scripts began.
entries.application: A showrunner holds episode-level breaking until the season map exists in at least outline form, because an early episode broken in detail against an unmapped season is often the first casualty of a later change of plan.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Bible as Selling Document vs Working Document
entries.description: A series bible written to sell a pitch and a series bible written to run a production are different documents even when they share a title.
entries.principle: Write the selling bible to persuade and the production bible to instruct — conflating the two produces a document that does neither job well.
entries.example: A pitch-stage bible commonly leads with tone, hook and comparable titles; a production bible written after a pickup instead documents world rules, character voice and format mechanics for a growing writing staff.
entries.application: A writer asked for the bible confirms which document is wanted before drafting, because a buyer wants to be sold and a new staff writer wants to be instructed.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Format Bible's Machine of Constraints
entries.description: A format show's bible documents the machine that generates each episode — the rules a new territory's licensee has to follow to reproduce the format.
entries.principle: Write the format bible as an instruction manual for the engine, not as a description of any one produced episode.
entries.example: Whose Line Is It Anyway? (Channel 4, 1988–1998 UK; ABC, 1998–2007 US) was sold internationally with a format bible documenting rules a new production has to reproduce, separate from any single aired episode.
entries.application: A writer drafting a format bible states the fixed rule and the variable within it separately, because a licensee needs to know exactly what may change between territories and what may not.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The World Document for a Returning Set
entries.description: A show built around a recurring location or institution documents that world's internal rules so later writers do not contradict earlier episodes by accident.
entries.principle: Record a returning world's fixed facts the first time they are established, because the fact a writer invents once becomes canon the room has to protect for the life of the show.
entries.example: ER's (1994–2009, NBC) hospital setting required a maintained internal document of medical procedure, staff hierarchy and physical geography so a large rotating writing staff would not contradict it episode to episode.
entries.application: A writer establishing a new world fact in a script flags it to the room's continuity keeper the same day, rather than trusting memory to carry it into next season.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Pilot as Tone Sample, Not Just First Episode
entries.description: A pilot script functions as a demonstration of the show's voice for a buyer as much as it functions as the first produced episode.
entries.principle: Write a pilot to prove the format can repeat, not only to tell its own best story — a pilot that only works once has not proven a series.
entries.example: A pilot that leans entirely on a premise's origin story — a death, an arrival, an inciting incident that cannot recur — risks proving the concept without proving the format that has to sustain it for a full order.
entries.application: A writer drafting a pilot pressure-tests it by asking what episode two looks like using the same engine, before finishing the polish pass on episode one.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: Backstory Reserved vs Discoverable on Screen
entries.description: A bible commonly holds more character history than any script will ever state on screen, kept in reserve for writers rather than for the audience.
entries.principle: Keep bible backstory available to the room without obligating any of it to appear on screen — reserved material is a resource, not a debt the scripts owe the audience.
entries.example: Lost's (2004–2010, ABC) writers maintained extensive character backstory documentation well beyond what any single flashback episode dramatized.
entries.application: A writer drafting a character's bible entry separates what the room must know from what the audience must eventually see, because treating every reserved fact as a future flashback obligation overloads the season order.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Procedural's Case-Machine Section
entries.description: A procedural's bible commonly documents the rules of its case-generating engine separately from its cast — how a case is structured, how it is solved, what the show's method looks like.
entries.principle: Document the case machine as its own section, distinct from character material, because a procedural's engine has to be reproducible by a freelance writer who has never met the cast.
entries.example: A crime procedural's bible typically specifies its investigative method — forensic, legal, medical — as a standalone section a new writer can consult without reading the character material at all.
entries.application: A writer pitching a freelance episode to a procedural reads the case-machine section of the bible first, because a case that violates the show's stated method will be rejected before its character work is even considered.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Continuing Drama's Never-Ending Bible
entries.description: A soap's bible is a living document updated indefinitely, unlike a limited series' bible, which is finished once the order is complete.
entries.principle: Maintain a continuing drama's bible as a permanently open document, because the show it describes has no announced ending to close it against.
entries.example: Coronation Street's (1960– , ITV) internal continuity records have been maintained and revised continuously across more than six decades of production.
entries.application: A continuity writer on a long-running soap treats the bible as a document that is never finished, only current, and schedules regular audits against it rather than trusting it stays accurate by default.

entries.category: The Bible and the Series Document
entries.name: The Pitch Deck vs the Production Bible
entries.description: A pitch deck is a short, visually led document built to win a commission; a production bible is a longer working reference built to run one once it exists.
entries.principle: Do not hand a buyer a production bible or hand a new staff writer a pitch deck — each document is built for a different reader at a different stage.
entries.example: Format pitch materials for shows such as Big Brother (1999– , Veronica then multiple broadcasters internationally) have circulated as short pitch decks preceding the fuller production bible that follows only once a licence is agreed.
entries.application: A writer preparing pitch materials keeps the deck to what a buyer needs to say yes, saving the mechanical detail a licensee will need later for the production bible instead.

entries.name: The Franchise Character Built to Survive Indefinitely
entries.description: A character designed for an open-ended series has to be built to keep generating story without using themselves up.
entries.principle: Design an open-ended series' lead around a renewable want, not a want a single story can satisfy and close.
entries.example: House's (2004–2012, Fox) title character is built around an unresolved need — being right — that no single case can ever finally satisfy, which is what let the format run eight seasons.
entries.application: A writer creating a returning-series lead checks whether the character's core want can be satisfied by the pilot's own plot; if it can, the want has to be rebuilt as something the series, not the pilot, resolves.

entries.name: The Ensemble's Rotation of Focus
entries.description: An ensemble show distributes its lead role across episodes rather than fixing it permanently on one character.
entries.principle: Plan an ensemble season so every regular gets an episode built around their want, not only the character the marketing favours.
entries.example: Cheers (1982–1993, NBC) rotated its A-plot lead across its bar-set ensemble episode to episode rather than centering every hour on the same character.
entries.application: A showrunner tracks focus distribution across a season on the same board used to track plot, because an ensemble that quietly stops rotating becomes a lead-and-supporting-cast show without ever deciding to.

entries.name: Character Stasis as Structural Necessity
entries.description: A sitcom character conventionally returns close to their starting point by the next episode, because the format depends on the premise resetting.
entries.principle: Protect a sitcom character's core condition from permanent change, because a format built to repeat cannot survive its own engine being solved.
entries.example: Homer Simpson's situation on The Simpsons (1989– , Fox) has been substantially unchanged across more than three decades precisely because the format depends on it staying that way.
entries.application: A writer pitching permanent change to a sitcom regular's situation checks whether the format can still generate its weekly engine afterward; if it cannot, the change belongs in a finale, not a mid-run episode.

entries.name: The Serialized Change Budget
entries.description: A serial drama's characters do change, but a season has a limited amount of change it can spend before the show becomes unrecognizable to a returning viewer.
entries.principle: Ration permanent character change across a season rather than spending it all in one arc, because a show with nothing left to change has nothing left to serialize.
entries.example: Breaking Bad (2008–2013, AMC) paced its lead's transformation across five seasons rather than several episodes, budgeting the change across the whole commissioned run.
entries.application: A showrunner maps a season's planned character changes against the whole series' arc before locking them, to confirm the season is not spending change the later seasons will need.

entries.name: Guest, Recurring, Regular: the Economics of Presence
entries.description: Three different contractual tiers of character presence, each carrying different costs and different story privileges.
entries.principle: Match a character's story weight to their contractual tier before writing them into a season arc, because a guest-tier actor's schedule cannot carry a regular-tier storyline.
entries.example: A character promoted from recurring to series regular — a common mid-run move across long-running dramas — typically follows a network or studio contract renegotiation, not only a creative decision.
entries.application: A writer proposing to expand a recurring character's role confirms the actor's contractual availability with production before breaking a story that assumes it.

entries.name: The Character-Wallpaper Problem of Long Runs
entries.description: A character who has appeared in hundreds of episodes risks becoming background furniture a room stops actively writing.
entries.principle: Re-audit a long-running character's want periodically, because a character nobody is actively writing toward becomes wallpaper even while still appearing every week.
entries.example: Ensemble procedurals running past ten seasons commonly rotate writers specifically tasked with reviving a supporting character's arc once it has gone quiet for multiple seasons.
entries.application: A showrunner schedules a periodic pass, commonly at a season's start, checking every regular character against a live, current want, and flags any character whose want has not moved in a full season.

entries.name: Character Death as Structural Event
entries.description: Killing a series regular is a production and contractual event as much as a story choice, and is usually driven by factors outside the writers' room.
entries.principle: Treat a regular's death as a decision the room proposes but production and network approve, because the story consequence is only one half of the decision.
entries.example: Character deaths on long-running procedurals and soaps are frequently reported as following an actor's own decision to leave, a contract dispute, or a network's cost decision, rather than originating purely in the writers' room.
entries.application: A writer pitching a character death confirms the production reality behind it before breaking the story consequences, because a death written to be reversible and a death that is contractually final require different aftermath plotting.

entries.name: The Spin-off Character Test
entries.description: Before a character is spun off into their own series, the format has to prove that character can generate a new engine independent of the parent show.
entries.principle: Test a spin-off candidate by asking what weekly engine they generate alone, not by how popular they are inside the parent show's ensemble.
entries.example: Frasier (1993–2004, NBC), spun off from Cheers (1982–1993, NBC), succeeded by building an entirely new premise and setting around its lead rather than transplanting the original bar-set engine.
entries.application: A writer developing a spin-off pitch designs a new premise engine for the character first, and treats the parent show's popularity as marketing, not as proof the new format works.

entries.name: Dialogue Written to Be Heard, Not Read
entries.description: Television dialogue is consumed by ear in real time, which places different demands on it than dialogue in prose meant to be read and re-read.
entries.principle: Read dialogue aloud before locking a draft, because a line that parses cleanly on the page can still be unintelligible spoken once, at speed, over a scene's sound design.
entries.example: Multi-camera sitcom scripts are routinely read aloud at the table specifically to test spoken clarity, a step prose fiction has no equivalent of.
entries.application: A writer cuts any line that requires the audience to silently reread it to parse, because a viewer cannot rewind broadcast television the way a reader can reread a page.

entries.name: The Laugh Line's Placement Before the Cut
entries.description: A sitcom joke's punchline is conventionally placed at the very end of a scene, timed to land just before a cut or an act break.
entries.principle: Put the punchline last in the scene, because a joke followed by more dialogue buries its own laugh under the next line.
entries.example: Multi-camera sitcoms filmed before a live audience, such as Frasier (1993–2004, NBC), are edited to leave room for audience laughter precisely because the punchline is placed to trigger it right before a cut.
entries.application: A writer polishing a comedy scene moves any line that follows a joke to before it, unless that line is itself a topper building on the same laugh.

entries.name: Standards and Practices as a Language Constraint
entries.description: A broadcast network's content-standards department vets scripts against a house standard for language and content before production, a constraint a premium or streaming platform does not apply the same way.
entries.principle: Know which platform's content standard governs a script before drafting dialogue, because a line cleared for one broadcaster may be flagged by another and cut regardless of how the scene reads.
entries.example: NYPD Blue (1993–2005, ABC) drew standards-and-practices scrutiny and public controversy over language and content that a premium-cable equivalent, such as The Sopranos (1999–2007, HBO), was never subject to.
entries.application: A writer drafting for a broadcast network keeps a running awareness of that network's content limits rather than writing toward a premium-platform standard and editing down afterward.

entries.name: The ADR Reality Behind the Page
entries.description: A meaningful amount of broadcast dialogue is re-recorded in post-production, automated dialogue replacement, for clarity, timing or content reasons, after the scene has already been shot.
entries.principle: Write dialogue knowing a line may need to survive being re-recorded to a locked picture later, and keep alternate phrasing available for lines likely to draw a content note.
entries.example: A network procedural's line flagged by standards and practices after a scene is shot is commonly resolved with an ADR replacement rather than a reshoot, a documented practice across US broadcast dramas such as Law & Order (1990–2010, NBC).
entries.application: A writer anticipating a contentious line drafts a milder alternate phrasing at the same time, so an ADR fix exists without a fresh writing pass under deadline pressure.

entries.name: The Table-Read Clock
entries.description: A script's read-aloud runtime at the table read is the real measure of episode length, more reliable than a page count.
entries.principle: Time the table read, not the page count, because spoken pacing — pauses, overlaps, a slow performer — routinely diverges from the page-to-minute rule of thumb a script assumes.
entries.example: The rough convention that one script page equals roughly one minute of screen time is treated across the industry as a starting estimate to be corrected at the table read, not a fixed law.
entries.application: A writer receiving table-read timing that runs long or short cuts or expands dialogue against that measured runtime, not against the original page count.

entries.name: Exposition Disguised as Argument
entries.description: A common technique for delivering information the audience needs without a character explaining it flatly — put the fact inside a disagreement between two characters who both already know it.
entries.principle: Deliver necessary exposition as something two characters are fighting about, not as something one character explains to a character who would already know it.
entries.example: Procedural dramas routinely deliver case background through a disagreement between two investigators about what the evidence means, rather than one restating known facts to the other.
entries.application: A writer who catches a character reminding another character of something they would already know rewrites the exchange as a live disagreement instead, so the same facts land as conflict rather than as a recap.

entries.name: The Setup-Punch-Tag Joke Rhythm
entries.description: A common three-beat comedy structure — a setup line, a punchline, and a tag line that extends or subverts the punchline for a second, smaller laugh.
entries.principle: Follow a punchline with a tag only when the tag earns its own laugh, because an unearned tag flattens the bigger laugh that came before it.
entries.example: Multi-camera sitcom scripts commonly mark tags explicitly in the room, testing at the table read whether the tag draws its own response or merely rides on the punchline's.
entries.application: A writer drafting a joke sequence cuts a weak tag rather than keeping it for rhythm, because a tag that does not land reads as the joke continuing past its own ending.

entries.name: The Idiom Problem in Territory Adaptation
entries.description: Dialogue written for one territory's idiom, slang and cultural reference commonly does not translate directly when a format or a script is adapted for another market.
entries.principle: Write local idiom knowing it will not survive direct translation, and separate the joke's structure from its specific wording so a licensed remake can rebuild the joke rather than merely translate it.
entries.example: A licensed sitcom remake commonly rewrites a joke's specific cultural reference for the new territory while preserving its underlying structure, rather than translating the original line word for word.
entries.application: A writer working on a format intended for international licensing marks which jokes depend on a culturally specific reference, so a remake's writers know which lines need rebuilding rather than translating.

entries.name: The Standing Set as a Story Engine
entries.description: A show's redressable, reusable sets are a budget decision that becomes a story asset once writers learn to generate plot from the location itself.
entries.principle: Treat a standing set as a story generator, not just a backdrop — a location built once and reused for years should be earning its keep in plot, not just hosting it.
entries.example: Cheers (1982–1993, NBC) built its entire run around a single standing bar set, turning a budget-driven decision into the show's defining structural asset.
