entries.awards: none — the first season competed as a drama, not a miniseries, at the 66th Primetime Emmy Awards, losing Outstanding Drama Series to Breaking Bad, though Cary Joji Fukunaga won Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series and the season won four additional Creative Arts Emmys including Outstanding Cinematography.
entries.description: The television series that restarts its entire cast, setting, and storyline each season while keeping only its title and Southern-noir sensibility,…
entries.text: The television series that restarts its entire cast, setting, and storyline each season while keeping only its title and Southern-noir sensibility, first commissioned by HBO and first broadcast January 12, 2014, created by Nic Pizzolatto. Its first season, directed in full by Cary Joji Fukunaga and starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson as Louisiana detectives investigating a decades-spanning case, was submitted to the Television Academy as a drama series rather than a miniseries that year, even though its season-to-season reset was structurally identical to the debut season of Fargo, which the Academy did recognize as a miniseries and awarded accordingly — a real inconsistency in how the same new anthology structure got classified twice in the same Emmy cycle.

entries.name: American Crime Story
entries.author: Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski
entries.awards: Nine Primetime Emmy Awards at the 68th ceremony for its first installment, The People v. O.J. Simpson, including Outstanding Limited Series.
entries.description: The television series that anthologizes real American criminal and political scandals into a new season-length dramatization each cycle, first…
entries.text: The television series that anthologizes real American criminal and political scandals into a new season-length dramatization each cycle, first commissioned by FX and first broadcast February 2, 2016, created by Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski with Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk as executive producers. Its first installment, The People v. O.J. Simpson, restaged the 1995 murder trial in close detail and won the Emmy for the format category its own executive producers had already built a reputation in with their earlier horror-fiction anthology American Horror Story, this time applying the reused-crew, new-story-each-season model to nonfiction subject matter instead.

entries.name: Chernobyl
entries.author: Craig Mazin
entries.awards: Outstanding Limited Series, Outstanding Directing for a Limited Series, and Outstanding Writing for a Limited Series at the 71st Primetime Emmy Awards; Best Miniseries or Television Film at the 77th Golden Globe Awards; Best Miniseries at the 2020 BAFTA TV Awards.
entries.description: The television series that dramatizes the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster and its cover-up across five episodes, each one built around a different…
entries.text: The television series that dramatizes the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster and its cover-up across five episodes, each one built around a different phase of the catastrophe and the scientists and workers who tried to contain it, first commissioned by HBO and first broadcast May 6, 2019, created by Craig Mazin. It swept that year's major limited-series awards across all three of the American, British, and international ceremonies it was eligible for — the Emmys, the Golden Globes, and the BAFTA TV Awards — an unusually complete sweep for a five-episode co-production between a premium American cable network and the UK's Sky Atlantic.

entries.name: Big Little Lies
entries.author: David E. Kelley
entries.awards: Outstanding Limited Series at the 69th Primetime Emmy Awards, plus acting wins for Nicole Kidman, Alexander Skarsgård, and Laura Dern, and Best Miniseries or Television Film at the 74th Golden Globe Awards.
entries.description: The television series that follows a group of Monterey, California mothers whose lives intersect around a murder revealed only in its final episode,…
entries.text: The television series that follows a group of Monterey, California mothers whose lives intersect around a murder revealed only in its final episode, first commissioned by HBO and first broadcast February 19, 2017, created by David E. Kelley from Liane Moriarty's novel. Marketed and awarded as a limited series in its first season, its December 2017 renewal for a second season — announced only after that year's awards voting had already closed — became a widely cited case study in how "limited series" could be used as a strategic, non-binding label, prompting the Producers Guild of America to reopen its own voting and reclassify the show as an ongoing drama.

entries.name: Sherlock
entries.author: Steven Moffat and Mark Gatiss
entries.awards: Best Drama Series at the 2011 BAFTA Television Awards; Outstanding Television Movie at the 68th Primetime Emmy Awards; three acting and writing Emmys at the 66th ceremony, including Outstanding Lead Actor for Benedict Cumberbatch.
entries.description: The television series that reimagines Arthur Conan Doyle's detective in modern London across feature-length episodes rather than a standard weekly…
entries.text: The television series that reimagines Arthur Conan Doyle's detective in modern London across feature-length episodes rather than a standard weekly runtime, first commissioned by BBC One and first broadcast July 25, 2010, created by Steven Moffat and Mark Gatiss. Each of its thirteen episodes across four series runs 85 to 90 minutes rather than the hour originally planned, a length the BBC itself requested mid-development, making the series one of the clearest cases in British television of a broadcaster's own scheduling decision reshaping a show's format after the fact.

entries.name: The Queen's Gambit
entries.author: Scott Frank
entries.awards: 11 Primetime Emmy Awards at the 73rd ceremony, including Outstanding Limited or Anthology Series and Outstanding Directing for a Limited or Anthology Series for Scott Frank.
entries.description: The television series that follows an orphaned chess prodigy's rise through the male-dominated competitive chess world of the 1950s and 1960s,…
entries.text: The television series that follows an orphaned chess prodigy's rise through the male-dominated competitive chess world of the 1950s and 1960s, adapted across seven episodes from Walter Tevis's 1983 novel, first released by Netflix on October 23, 2020, created by Scott Frank. Its release measurably moved a hobby industry's real-world sales: chess set manufacturers and secondhand booksellers reported sold-out stock within weeks, and Chess.com and other online chess platforms recorded some of the largest sign-up surges in their history, a rare case of a scripted limited series' cultural reach showing up directly in another industry's numbers.

entries.name: Olive Kitteridge
entries.author: Jane Anderson
entries.awards: Eight Primetime Emmy Awards at the 67th ceremony, including Outstanding Limited Series, Outstanding Lead Actress for Frances McDormand, and Outstanding Lead Actor for Richard Jenkins.
entries.description: The television series that adapts Elizabeth Strout's linked short-story collection into a four-part portrait of one difficult, unsentimental Maine…
entries.text: The television series that adapts Elizabeth Strout's linked short-story collection into a four-part portrait of one difficult, unsentimental Maine schoolteacher across nearly three decades of her own marriage, first commissioned by HBO and first broadcast November 2, 2014, adapted by Jane Anderson. Airing two of its four episodes back-to-back on each of two consecutive nights rather than spacing all four across separate weeks, it compressed a story spanning almost thirty fictional years into a single condensed broadcast event, then won that year's top Emmy for the category outright — a literary character study, with no crime, disaster, or courtroom driving its plot, taking the format's biggest prize over more incident-heavy competition.

entries.name: When They See Us
entries.author: Ava DuVernay
entries.awards: Peabody Award, 2020; Outstanding Lead Actor in a Limited Series or Movie for Jharrel Jerome at the 71st Primetime Emmy Awards.
entries.description: The television series that dramatizes the wrongful 1989 conviction and eventual 2002 exoneration of five Harlem teenagers falsely accused in the…
entries.text: The television series that dramatizes the wrongful 1989 conviction and eventual 2002 exoneration of five Harlem teenagers falsely accused in the Central Park jogger case, first released by Netflix in four parts on May 31, 2019, created and directed by Ava DuVernay. Jerome's win made him the youngest actor ever to win the lead-actor Emmy in that category and the first Afro-Latino actor to win any acting Emmy, and the broadcast itself renewed public scrutiny of the real case: the lead prosecutor lost her publishing deal and resigned from a nonprofit board amid the backlash, while the still-living men the series was about had already had their convictions vacated in 2002 after the actual perpetrator confessed.

entries.name: Roots
entries.author: Alex Haley
entries.awards: Nine Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Limited Series.
entries.description: The television series that dramatizes seven generations of one Black American family across slavery, the Civil War, and Reconstruction, adapted by…
entries.text: The television series that dramatizes seven generations of one Black American family across slavery, the Civil War, and Reconstruction, adapted by Alex Haley from his own researched account of his family's history, first commissioned by ABC and first broadcast over eight consecutive nights beginning January 23, 1977. Its finale alone drew an estimated 100 million viewers, with the full run averaging around 80 million a night, among the largest audiences ever recorded for American television; ABC's decision to air all eight episodes on consecutive nights rather than spacing them weekly became the founding example of the now-standard "event miniseries" broadcast strategy.

entries.name: Band of Brothers
entries.author: Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks
entries.awards: Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Miniseries and six additional Emmys at the 53rd ceremony; Golden Globe Award for Best Miniseries or Motion Picture Made for Television.
entries.description: The television series that follows a single U.S. Army parachute infantry company from training through the end of World War II in Europe, based on…
entries.text: The television series that follows a single U.S. Army parachute infantry company from training through the end of World War II in Europe, based on Stephen Ambrose's history of the unit, first commissioned by HBO and broadcast in ten parts from September 9 to November 4, 2001, executive produced by Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks. Its reported production cost of more than $125 million made it, at the time, one of the most expensive television productions ever made, setting a feature-film-scale production-value benchmark that later prestige war and history miniseries were measured against.

entries.name: Watchmen
entries.author: Damon Lindelof
entries.awards: 11 Primetime Emmy Awards at the 72nd ceremony, including Outstanding Limited Series, Outstanding Lead Actress for Regina King, and Outstanding Supporting Actor for Yahya Abdul-Mateen II.
entries.description: The television series that continues the story of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's 1986-87 comic as a sequel set decades later in an alternate present,…
entries.text: The television series that continues the story of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's 1986-87 comic as a sequel set decades later in an alternate present, opening its first episode with a dramatization of the real 1921 Tulsa race massacre, first commissioned by HBO and first broadcast October 20, 2019, created by Damon Lindelof. Announced without a stated commitment to a second season, HBO confirmed after its run that the story would not continue without Lindelof's direct involvement and formally reclassified the work as a limited series, settling the same billing tension — an ambiguous label resolved only after the fact — that Big Little Lies had already made a public case study of two years earlier.

entries.name: I May Destroy You
entries.author: Michaela Coel
entries.awards: Best Mini-Series, Best Actress for Michaela Coel, Best Director: Drama, and Best Writer: Drama at the 2021 BAFTA Television Awards; Outstanding Writing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards.
entries.description: The television series that follows a novelist reconstructing a night she was drugged and sexually assaulted, drawing directly on Michaela Coel's own…
entries.text: The television series that follows a novelist reconstructing a night she was drugged and sexually assaulted, drawing directly on Michaela Coel's own experience, first broadcast by HBO in the United States on June 7, 2020, one day ahead of its BBC One broadcast in the UK, created, written, and co-directed by Coel. Coel turned down a reported $1 million offer from Netflix specifically because the deal would have required her to give up a share of the show's copyright, keeping full creative and ownership control instead through the smaller BBC/HBO deal — a widely cited case study in format-ownership terms shaping a creator's choice of broadcaster.

entries.name: The Format Age: Television's Entertainment Revolution
entries.author: Jean K. Chalaby
entries.awards: None documented — a trade-academic press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks; earlier drafting notes for this pack had wrongly attached an "International Emmy for Outstanding Scholarship" to this title, an award category that does not exist, and this card corrects that rather than repeating it.
entries.description: The study that argues the television format — a licensed, adaptable programme template rather than a finished show — became a genuine industry of…
entries.text: The study that argues the television format — a licensed, adaptable programme template rather than a finished show — became a genuine industry of its own only from the late 1990s onward, built from interviews with the format trade's own creators and dealmakers rather than from audience research alone. Chalaby, a City University London sociologist, traces the business infrastructure behind formats crossing borders: the production companies, licensing deal shapes, and power struggles between originating and adapting territories that decide which formats travel and which do not, making it the standard reference work this pack's own International Formats and Their Remakes category draws on most directly.

entries.name: Global Television Formats: Understanding Television Across Borders
entries.author: Tasha Oren and Sharon Shahaf (eds.)
entries.awards: None documented — an academic essay collection outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that collects essays from format scholars across multiple countries rather than arguing a single thesis, first published by Routledge in…
entries.text: The study that collects essays from format scholars across multiple countries rather than arguing a single thesis, first published by Routledge in 2012, edited by Tasha Oren and Sharon Shahaf. Its chapters work case by case — a format examined in its country of origin, then again in one or more markets it was licensed into — building a comparative method for reading the same licensed template against a different national broadcasting culture and audience each time, useful specifically where this pack's International Formats category needed to weigh a remake's changes against its original rather than treat either version as the default.

entries.name: TV Formats Worldwide: Localizing Global Programs
entries.author: Albert Moran (ed.)
entries.awards: None documented — an academic essay collection outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that collects case studies of specific format licensing deals territory by territory, first published by Intellect Books in 2009, edited…
entries.text: The study that collects case studies of specific format licensing deals territory by territory, first published by Intellect Books in 2009, edited by Albert Moran, one of the field's earliest and most cited format scholars. Its chapters work from trade press records and interviews with the licensing companies themselves rather than from the finished broadcasts, tracking how a format's contract terms, not just its on-screen content, are what actually gets sold and renegotiated each time it crosses into a new market.

entries.name: Copycat TV: Globalisation, Program Formats and Cultural Identity
entries.author: Albert Moran
entries.awards: None documented — an academic monograph outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that made the early scholarly case for treating the licensed program format, rather than the individual finished broadcast, as…
entries.text: The study that made the early scholarly case for treating the licensed program format, rather than the individual finished broadcast, as television's real unit of globalization, first published in 1998 through the University of Luton Press. Written solely by Albert Moran rather than co-authored — a fact worth stating plainly, since this book is sometimes conflated in citation with his later, genuinely co-authored "Understanding the Global TV Format" — it predates most of the field it went on to found, making it a founding rather than a synthesizing text.

entries.name: Understanding the Global TV Format
entries.author: Albert Moran and Justin Malbon
entries.awards: None documented — a trade-academic press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that catalogues the format industry's own working vocabulary — bible, tone, template, look — and matches each term to what it actually…
entries.text: The study that catalogues the format industry's own working vocabulary — bible, tone, template, look — and matches each term to what it actually controls in a licensing contract, first published by Intellect Books in 2009, co-written by Albert Moran and Justin Malbon. Malbon's own background in law shapes the book's central usefulness: it reads formats as intellectual-property instruments first, treating the on-screen program as the visible surface of an underlying contract a novelist researching format television would otherwise never see.

entries.name: The Television Genre Book
entries.author: Glen Creeber (ed.)
entries.awards: None documented — an academic reference anthology outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that organizes the entire medium by genre rather than by history or nation, assembling short essays from dozens of television scholars on…
entries.text: The study that organizes the entire medium by genre rather than by history or nation, assembling short essays from dozens of television scholars on individual genres from the soap opera to the quiz show, first published by the British Film Institute, now in its third edition as of 2015 under editor Glen Creeber. Each entry is written by a different specialist in that specific genre rather than by Creeber generalizing across all of them, giving the collection a range of individual critical voices no single-author genre history could match.

entries.name: Reality TV: Realism and Revelation
entries.author: Anita Biressi and Heather Nunn
entries.awards: None documented — an academic monograph outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that reads reality television's confessional and observational formats as a continuation of documentary realism's own claims to…
entries.text: The study that reads reality television's confessional and observational formats as a continuation of documentary realism's own claims to authenticity rather than as documentary's opposite or debasement, first published by Wallflower Press in 2005. Biressi and Nunn place formats like structured-reality docusoaps and makeover shows inside a much older tradition of factual British broadcasting, arguing that the genre's most-mocked conventions — the confessional interview, the fly-on-the-wall camera — are direct descendants of documentary technique rather than a modern debasement of it.

entries.name: Difficult Men: Behind the Scenes of a Creative Revolution
entries.author: Brett Martin
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that names and dates American television's "Third Golden Age" — the run of serialized cable dramas from The Sopranos through Breaking Bad…
entries.text: The study that names and dates American television's "Third Golden Age" — the run of serialized cable dramas from The Sopranos through Breaking Bad — and argues the shows themselves cannot be separated from the volatile, often abusive showrunners who made them, first published by Penguin Press in 2013. Martin's reporting draws on direct access to the writers' rooms of The Sopranos, The Wire, Mad Men, and Breaking Bad, and the book's title is a deliberate double meaning: difficult men made the shows, and difficult men are what most of the shows were about.

entries.name: Top of the Rock: Inside the Rise and Fall of Must See TV
entries.author: Warren Littlefield with T.R. Pearson
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that reconstructs NBC's Thursday-night "Must See TV" era — Friends, Seinfeld, Frasier, ER, and the block-programming strategy built around…
entries.text: The study that reconstructs NBC's Thursday-night "Must See TV" era — Friends, Seinfeld, Frasier, ER, and the block-programming strategy built around them — entirely from first-person oral history rather than outside analysis, first published by Doubleday in 2012. Written by Warren Littlefield, the NBC entertainment president who built that schedule himself, the book assembles competing memories from writers, actors, and executives without smoothing over where their accounts of the same decisions actually disagree.

entries.name: Showrunners: The Art of Running a TV Show
entries.author: Tara Bennett
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press companion title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study built as the official companion book to Des Doyle's 2014 documentary of the same name, first published by Titan Books, gathering extended…
entries.text: The study built as the official companion book to Des Doyle's 2014 documentary of the same name, first published by Titan Books, gathering extended interviews with working showrunners including Bill Prady, David Shore, Joss Whedon, and Ronald D. Moore that the film itself had no room to include in full. Assembled by television journalist Tara Bennett from the documentary's own raw interview footage rather than freshly conducted, the book functions as the extended director's-cut transcript of a project that was a film first and a book only afterward.

entries.name: The Revolution Was Televised
entries.author: Alan Sepinwall
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that traces the rise of serialized, novelistic American drama through twelve shows Sepinwall argues built it — The Sopranos, The Wire,…
entries.text: The study that traces the rise of serialized, novelistic American drama through twelve shows Sepinwall argues built it — The Sopranos, The Wire, Deadwood, The Shield, Lost, Battlestar Galactica, Friday Night Lights, Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and others — first self-published by Sepinwall himself in 2012 before Touchstone, an imprint of Simon & Schuster, acquired and reissued an expanded edition in 2013. Sepinwall's own critical method, developed on his blog reviewing shows episode by episode as they aired rather than waiting for a season's end, is the book's implicit case for why this era's television rewarded that kind of close, week-to-week attention in the first place.

entries.name: Television and the Meaning of "Live": An Enquiry into the Human Situation
entries.author: Paddy Scannell
entries.awards: None documented — an academic monograph outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that argues live broadcasting's access to an unfolding "now" is not a technical feature of television but a basic condition of human…
entries.text: The study that argues live broadcasting's access to an unfolding "now" is not a technical feature of television but a basic condition of human experience the medium happens to make newly visible, first published by Polity Press in 2014. Scannell, drawing on phenomenology rather than industry history, treats liveness as older than television itself — a claim distinct from and easily confused with work on the same subject by other media scholars, including Jérôme Bourdon, whose own writing on liveness this pack's earlier drafting notes had mistakenly credited with this specific title before the correction was caught and made.

entries.name: Makeover Television: Realities Remodelled
entries.author: Dana Heller (ed.)
entries.awards: None documented — an academic essay collection outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that collects essays on makeover formats — home renovation, cosmetic surgery, style and etiquette conversion, and their international…
entries.text: The study that collects essays on makeover formats — home renovation, cosmetic surgery, style and etiquette conversion, and their international variants — as a single category of television built specifically to intervene in ordinary lives rather than merely document them, first published by I.B. Tauris in 2007, edited by Dana Heller. Its contributors read the format's promise of transformation across several different kinds of remodeling at once — of houses, of bodies, of taste, of visible class status — as versions of the same underlying televisual claim: that watched change is itself the entertainment.

entries.name: Media Events: The Live Broadcasting of History
entries.author: Daniel Dayan and Elihu Katz
entries.awards: None documented — an academic monograph outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that coined the term "media events" for the specific class of live broadcast — a state funeral, a royal wedding, a moon landing, a live…
entries.text: The study that coined the term "media events" for the specific class of live broadcast — a state funeral, a royal wedding, a moon landing, a live contest final — that interrupts a broadcaster's own routine schedule and briefly commands an entire national or global audience's shared attention at once, first published by Harvard University Press in 1992. Dayan and Katz sort these events into three named categories — Contests, Conquests, and Coronations — a taxonomy this pack's own reality-competition finale cards and appointment-viewing psychology cards both draw on directly when explaining why a single broadcast can matter more than the sum of the ratings points it earns.

entries.name: The Television Will Be Revolutionized
entries.author: Amanda D. Lotz
entries.awards: None documented — a trade-academic press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that argues the American broadcast "network era" of scheduled, appointment-only viewing had already ended by the mid-2000s, replaced by a…
entries.text: The study that argues the American broadcast "network era" of scheduled, appointment-only viewing had already ended by the mid-2000s, replaced by a "post-network era" in which the DVR, on-demand delivery, and eventually streaming shifted real control over when and how a show gets watched from the network to the viewer, first published by NYU Press in 2007, written by Amanda D. Lotz. A second edition in 2014 extended the same argument through the first wave of Netflix and Hulu original programming, treating streaming not as a new disruption but as the post-network shift's next, entirely predictable stage.

entries.name: Cable Cowboy: John Malone and the Rise of the Modern Cable Business
entries.author: Mark Robichaux
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that follows cable executive John Malone's build-out of Tele-Communications Inc. from a struggling regional operator into the dominant…
entries.text: The study that follows cable executive John Malone's build-out of Tele-Communications Inc. from a struggling regional operator into the dominant force in American cable television, first published by John Wiley & Sons in 2002, written by former Wall Street Journal reporter Mark Robichaux. The book traces the deregulation-era deal-making that let Malone consolidate cable systems nationwide and, through TCI's stake in what became Discovery and other channels, quietly control much of the programming carried on wires he did not always own outright — the business history behind the cable channels this pack's other categories treat as simply always having existed.

entries.name: The Box: An Oral History of Television, 1920-1961
entries.author: Jeff Kisseloff
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study built entirely from first-person interviews with the engineers, executives, and performers who worked in American television before the…
entries.text: The study built entirely from first-person interviews with the engineers, executives, and performers who worked in American television before the medium had settled into any of its later genre conventions, first published by Viking Penguin in 1995, compiled by Jeff Kisseloff. Because Kisseloff conducted these interviews decades after the events they describe but before most of these subjects had died, the book preserves testimony — about live 1930s mechanical-television experiments, wartime broadcast shutdowns, and the earliest commercial variety programming — that has no equivalent primary-source record anywhere else.

entries.name: Stealing the Show: How Women Are Revolutionizing Television
entries.author: Joy Press
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that profiles the women showrunners — including Shonda Rhimes, Jenji Kohan, Lena Dunham, Mindy Kaling, and Tina Fey — who built or ran…
entries.text: The study that profiles the women showrunners — including Shonda Rhimes, Jenji Kohan, Lena Dunham, Mindy Kaling, and Tina Fey — who built or ran some of American television's most-discussed shows of the 2000s and 2010s, first published by Atria Books, an imprint of Simon & Schuster, in 2018, written by former Village Voice critic Joy Press. Press argues these showrunners changed American television's actual subject matter as much as its production hierarchy, putting female ambition, female anger, and female sexuality on screen in ways broadcast-network television had specifically avoided for the previous several decades.

entries.name: Tube of Plenty: The Evolution of American Television
entries.author: Erik Barnouw
entries.awards: None documented for this title specifically — Barnouw's own broader career includes a 1944 Peabody Award and a 1971 George Polk Award for his documentary filmmaking, and the Organization of American Historians has given an award named for him since 1983, but none of those attach to this particular book.
entries.description: The study that condenses Barnouw's own multi-volume scholarly history of American broadcasting into a single continuous narrative of commercial…
entries.text: The study that condenses Barnouw's own multi-volume scholarly history of American broadcasting into a single continuous narrative of commercial television's growth, first published by Oxford University Press in 1975 and revised in 1990 to extend the account into the cable era. Barnouw, a Columbia University professor and himself an award-winning documentary filmmaker — a winner of both a Peabody and a George Polk Award — rather than only an academic historian of the medium, wrote from a vantage point close enough to television's first three decades that much of the book functions as a witness account as much as a scholarly one.

entries.name: Reality Bites Back: The Troubling Truth About Guilty Pleasure TV
entries.author: Jennifer L. Pozner
entries.awards: None documented — a trade press title outside the prize tracks this pack otherwise checks.
entries.description: The study that argues unscripted television's editing and casting choices actively construct the sexist, racist, and classist storylines they are…
entries.text: The study that argues unscripted television's editing and casting choices actively construct the sexist, racist, and classist storylines they are usually assumed to simply capture, first published by Seal Press in 2010, written by media critic and Women's Media Center founder Jennifer L. Pozner. Pozner's own term for one of the format's core editing techniques — "Frankenbiting," splicing unrelated lines of a contestant's own speech together into a sentence they never actually said — names a specific, still widely used production practice this pack's own reality-competition cards otherwise describe only in terms of its effects, not its method.

entries.name: Hancock's Half Hour
entries.author: Ray Galton and Alan Simpson
entries.awards: None documented for this radio series specifically — the later television adaptation of the same title won a 1962 Jacob's Award in Ireland and placed 24th on the BFI's "100 Greatest British Television Programmes" list in 2000, but those accolades attach to the TV version, not this radio original.
entries.description: The radio programme that built an entire half hour around one continuing character's own delusions of grandeur and repeated small humiliations…
entries.text: The radio programme that built an entire half hour around one continuing character's own delusions of grandeur and repeated small humiliations rather than around a rotating cast of sketches and guest turns, first broadcast by the BBC on November 2, 1954, written by Ray Galton and Alan Simpson and starring Tony Hancock. Whether it or an American predecessor actually originated the sitcom is a genuinely contested question this card does not settle: American broadcast historians typically point to The Goldbergs (1929) and Amos 'n' Andy (1928), both over two decades earlier, as the form's true origin, while some British historians credit still-earlier native British radio comedies with establishing the half-hour narrative-sitcom format before Hancock's Half Hour arrived, crediting Galton and Simpson instead with a specific achievement — sustaining a single, fully interior comic character across an entire series — rather than with inventing the format outright.

entries.name: The Goon Show
entries.author: Spike Milligan
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that abandoned the sketch-and-gag structure of prior British radio comedy for surreal, non-sequitur storylines built from absurd…
entries.text: The radio programme that abandoned the sketch-and-gag structure of prior British radio comedy for surreal, non-sequitur storylines built from absurd sound effects and characters who existed mainly as voices doing impossible things, first broadcast by the BBC Home Service in May 1951 under the title "Crazy People," written principally by Spike Milligan. Its audience grew from roughly 370,000 listeners to nearly two million by its seventeenth episode, and its influence reached far beyond radio comedy itself: the Beatles, Monty Python, and the American Firesign Theatre have all named it as a direct influence on their own absurdist styles.

entries.name: The Goldbergs
entries.author: Gertrude Berg
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that followed a Jewish immigrant family's ordinary domestic life and neighborhood relationships rather than the melodrama…
entries.text: The radio programme that followed a Jewish immigrant family's ordinary domestic life and neighborhood relationships rather than the melodrama typical of other serialized "soap" programmes of its era, devised by Gertrude Berg in 1928 and sold to NBC, first broadcast as "The Rise of the Goldbergs" on November 20, 1929. Its focus on everyday, low-stakes family situations rather than crisis-driven plotting is the reason American broadcast historians frequently cite it, alongside Amos 'n' Andy, as one of the two competing points of origin for the situation comedy as a form — a claim this pack's Hancock's Half Hour card carries as one live side of a still-unsettled dispute rather than as settled fact.

entries.name: Amos 'n' Andy
entries.author: Freeman Gosden and Charles Correll
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that followed two Black characters through serialized, sitcom-length daily storylines, performed by two white actors, Freeman…
entries.text: The radio programme that followed two Black characters through serialized, sitcom-length daily storylines, performed by two white actors, Freeman Gosden and Charles Correll, working in the minstrel-dialect tradition, first broadcast on Chicago's WMAQ on March 19, 1928, before moving to NBC's Blue Network on August 19, 1929. The show's racial caricature drew sustained, organized opposition from the start: Bishop W. J. Walls publicly denounced its dialect and characterization in December 1930, the Pittsburgh Courier gathered more than 700,000 signatures on a 1931 petition to the Federal Radio Commission over it, and the NAACP formally protested its 1951 television adaptation as reinforcing the belief that Black people were "inferior, lazy, dumb, and dishonest" — a protest campaign that, combined with the civil rights movement, led CBS to withdraw the series from distribution entirely in 1966.

entries.name: Take It or Leave It
entries.author: CBS Radio (deviser not individually credited in the surviving record)
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that doubled a contestant's prize money with every question answered correctly, starting at one dollar and capping at…
entries.text: The radio programme that doubled a contestant's prize money with every question answered correctly, starting at one dollar and capping at sixty-four, first broadcast on CBS on April 21, 1940, with Bob Hawk as the first of five hosts across its decade on the air. No surviving record credits an individual deviser for its escalating-stakes format, but its mechanic is the direct and openly acknowledged model for the 1950s television quiz show The $64,000 Question, whose very title is the ceiling this programme first set.

entries.name: Twenty Questions
entries.author: Mutual Broadcasting System (deviser not individually credited in the surviving record)
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme built entirely on a panel trying to identify a listener-submitted subject using no more than twenty yes-or-no questions, first…
entries.text: The radio programme built entirely on a panel trying to identify a listener-submitted subject using no more than twenty yes-or-no questions, first broadcast at 8 p.m. on Saturday, February 2, 1946, from New York's Longacre Theatre on the Mutual Broadcasting System. Winston Churchill's cigar was, by a wide margin, the single most frequently submitted subject in the show's run, a small but telling measure of how much of its era's popular imagination it managed to absorb into a parlour-game format that later panel and guessing-game television formats inherited directly.

entries.name: Quiz Kids
entries.author: Louis G. Cowan
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that put a rotating panel of unusually accomplished children up against difficult adult-level questions for a live studio and…
entries.text: The radio programme that put a rotating panel of unusually accomplished children up against difficult adult-level questions for a live studio and home audience, created by Chicago advertising man Louis G. Cowan and first broadcast on NBC from Chicago on June 28, 1940, as a summer replacement show. Cowan went on to produce the 1950s television quiz show The $64,000 Question and later became president of CBS Television in 1958, only to be forced out the following year when the decade's quiz-show-rigging scandals broke — even though, by CBS's own later account, he had sold his production company years earlier and had no evidence of any knowledge of the rigging himself.

entries.name: Information Please
entries.author: Dan Golenpaul
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme believed to be the earliest example of the panel-game format — a standing panel of experts fielding questions sent in by…
entries.text: The radio programme believed to be the earliest example of the panel-game format — a standing panel of experts fielding questions sent in by listeners, playing for wit and wordplay as much as for correct answers — created by Dan Golenpaul and first broadcast on NBC on May 17, 1938. Its regular panelists, including pianist and wit Oscar Levant, ran for over a decade opposite a changing lineup of celebrity guests, establishing the durable trivia-panel structure that both radio and television quiz and panel formats have repeated ever since, often without any direct memory of this show as their common ancestor.

entries.name: Desert Island Discs
entries.author: Roy Plomley
entries.awards: Named the single greatest radio programme of all time by a panel of broadcasting industry experts, February 2019.
entries.description: The radio programme that asks one guest each episode to choose the eight recordings, one book, and one luxury item they would want if stranded on a…
entries.text: The radio programme that asks one guest each episode to choose the eight recordings, one book, and one luxury item they would want if stranded on a desert island, devised and originally presented by Roy Plomley, first broadcast on the BBC Forces Programme on January 29, 1942. It is still broadcasting today, more than eighty years and over 3,400 episodes later, on BBC Radio 4 — a longevity record this pack's other still-running-format cards can point to as the outer limit of what a single unchanged format premise can sustain.

entries.name: Workers' Playtime
entries.author: BBC Home Service, produced with Bill Gates and Margaret Everest
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme broadcast live three times a week from a different factory canteen "somewhere in Britain," never named on air for wartime…
entries.text: The radio programme broadcast live three times a week from a different factory canteen "somewhere in Britain," never named on air for wartime security reasons, first broadcast by the BBC Home Service and Forces Programme on May 31, 1941. Its stated purpose was morale, not comedy for its own sake — the Ministry of Labour itself chose which factories the show visited — and it stayed on the air for twenty-three years after the war it was built to sustain had already ended, outlasting the wartime justification for its own format by nearly two decades.

entries.name: It's That Man Again
entries.author: Ted Kavanagh and Tommy Handley
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme built around a fast-moving cast of catchphrase-driven recurring characters — Mrs Mopp's "Can I do you now, sir?," Colonel…
entries.text: The radio programme built around a fast-moving cast of catchphrase-driven recurring characters — Mrs Mopp's "Can I do you now, sir?," Colonel Chinstrap's "I don't mind if I do," the supposed German spy Funf — rather than a single continuing storyline, co-written by Tommy Handley and Ted Kavanagh and produced by Francis Worsley, first broadcast on the BBC on July 12, 1939. Widely credited as the most successful comedy series broadcast in Britain during the Second World War, its catchphrases became common currency well beyond its own listenership, functioning as the deliberately escapist entertainment the BBC leaned on to sustain morale through the Blitz.

entries.name: Suspense
entries.author: William Spier
entries.awards: None documented — a radio programme predating the relevant broadcast-award categories.
entries.description: The radio programme that dropped an ordinary person into a single threatening or bizarre situation each week and withheld the resolution until the…
entries.text: The radio programme that dropped an ordinary person into a single threatening or bizarre situation each week and withheld the resolution until the last possible moment, first tested as a single pilot episode on July 22, 1940 — an adaptation of "The Lodger" directed by Alfred Hitchcock as part of CBS's anthology tryout series Forecast — before William Spier developed it into a regular weekly CBS series beginning June 17, 1942. Running some 945 episodes over twenty years and casting major Hollywood film stars in radio-only thriller roles, its end in 1962 is frequently cited as the point at which American radio's own Golden Age of original drama effectively closed.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Duel
entries.author: Steven Spielberg
entries.awards: Nominated for two 1972 Primetime Emmy Awards (Outstanding Directing and Outstanding Writing, both for a Limited Series, Movie or Dramatic Special) and a Golden Globe Award; won neither.
entries.description: The television film that stages an entire feature-length thriller as one anonymous commuter's escalating roadside standoff with an unseen, wordless…
entries.text: The television film that stages an entire feature-length thriller as one anonymous commuter's escalating roadside standoff with an unseen, wordless truck driver, written by Richard Matheson from his own short story — itself based on a real tailgating incident Matheson experienced on a California highway in 1963 — and directed by 27-year-old Steven Spielberg, first broadcast on ABC on November 13, 1971. Its success on television led Universal to release an extended theatrical cut internationally the following year, launching Spielberg's feature-film career from what had begun as an assignment inside the network's own ABC Movie of the Week slot rather than as an independent production.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Brian's Song
entries.author: Buzz Kulik
entries.awards: Five Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Single Program – Drama or Comedy and Outstanding Supporting Actor (Jack Warden), plus a Peabody Award, a Directors Guild of America Award, and a Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Composition for Michel Legrand's score.
entries.description: The television film that dramatizes the friendship between Chicago Bears running backs Gale Sayers and Brian Piccolo — the NFL's first Black and…
entries.text: The television film that dramatizes the friendship between Chicago Bears running backs Gale Sayers and Brian Piccolo — the NFL's first Black and white roommates — through Piccolo's diagnosis with and death from cancer at age twenty-six, written by William Blinn and directed by Buzz Kulik, first broadcast on ABC on November 30, 1971. It was the most-watched television film of 1971, drawing a 32.9 Nielsen rating and a 48 percent audience share, and its combination of sports drama, interracial friendship, and terminal illness became the direct template later "guy-cry" sports films and disease-of-the-week television films have drawn on since.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: That Certain Summer
entries.author: Lamont Johnson
entries.awards: Scott Jacoby won a Primetime Emmy Award for his performance as the teenage son; the film also received Golden Globe and Directors Guild of America nominations, and was inducted into the Producers Guild of America's Hall of Fame in 1998.
entries.description: The television film that has a divorced father tell his teenage son he is gay and living with another man, rather than treating the disclosure…
entries.text: The television film that has a divorced father tell his teenage son he is gay and living with another man, rather than treating the disclosure itself as the plot's climax, written by Richard Levinson and William Link and directed by Lamont Johnson, first broadcast on ABC on November 1, 1972, starring Hal Holbrook and Martin Sheen. Contemporary reviewers, including The New York Times, praised its refusal of "melodrama, moralizing or convenient resolutions," and it is widely credited as American television's first sympathetic dramatization of a gay relationship — arriving more than a year before the American Psychiatric Association's board voted to remove homosexuality from its list of mental disorders.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Trilogy of Terror
entries.author: Dan Curtis
entries.awards: No contemporary Emmy or Golden Globe recognition; retrospectively ranked the fourth-greatest television film ever made by Complex (2011) and named television's scariest film by MeTV (2016), and nominated for Blockbuster Movie of the Week at the 2006 TV Land Awards.
entries.description: The television film that anthologizes three unconnected Richard Matheson stories around a single star, Karen Black, playing a different woman in…
entries.text: The television film that anthologizes three unconnected Richard Matheson stories around a single star, Karen Black, playing a different woman in each — culminating in "Amelia," in which a Zuni fetish doll's restraining chain falls off and the wooden hunter figure comes alive to stalk her apartment — directed by Dan Curtis and adapted for television by William F. Nolan and Matheson himself, first broadcast on ABC on March 4, 1975. The Zuni doll segment alone, only about twenty-five minutes of the ninety-minute broadcast, became one of American television's most reliably cited childhood-fright touchstones, outliving the two anthology segments broadcast alongside it in the public memory of the film.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Sybil
entries.author: Daniel Petrie
entries.awards: Sally Field won the 1977 Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited Series; the production received additional Emmy nominations.
entries.description: The television film that dramatizes psychiatrist Cornelia Wilbur's real-world treatment of a patient later publicized, under the pseudonym "Sybil,"…
entries.text: The television film that dramatizes psychiatrist Cornelia Wilbur's real-world treatment of a patient later publicized, under the pseudonym "Sybil," as having sixteen distinct personalities, written by Stewart Stern from Flora Rheta Schreiber's 1973 book and directed by Daniel Petrie, first broadcast over two nights on NBC on November 14 and 15, 1976, starring Sally Field opposite Joanne Woodward. Whether the underlying case was what the film presents is a dispute this card does not settle: journalist Debbie Nathan's 2011 book "Sybil Exposed," drawing on Wilbur's own case files and the patient's later letters, argued Wilbur's hypnosis and suggestive questioning substantially constructed the sixteen-personality account rather than uncovering it, while other clinicians and historians of the case have maintained the original diagnosis was genuine even if imperfectly documented — a dispute that has not stopped the film and book from being widely credited with the sharp rise in diagnoses of dissociative identity disorder through the late 1970s and 1980s.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Battlestar Galactica (1978 film)
entries.author: Richard A. Colla
entries.awards: Won the 1979 Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Creative Technical Crafts for its visual effects, and was nominated for Outstanding Art Direction for a Series.
entries.description: The television film that served as the three-hour pilot for creator Glen A. Larson's space-opera series, following a fleet of human survivors…
entries.text: The television film that served as the three-hour pilot for creator Glen A. Larson's space-opera series, following a fleet of human survivors fleeing an extinction-level attack by the robotic Cylons in search of a lost thirteenth colony called Earth, directed by Richard A. Colla (with additional scenes by Alan J. Levi) and first broadcast on ABC on September 17, 1978, its broadcast briefly interrupted so the network could announce the signing of the Camp David Accords. Budgeted at roughly eight million dollars, among the most expensive television productions of its era, it was also released as an edited theatrical feature abroad before its American broadcast, and its ratings success led ABC to order a weekly series before the format had even been tested as one.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: The Day After
entries.author: Nicholas Meyer
entries.awards: Won two Primetime Emmy Awards, for Outstanding Film Sound Editing and Outstanding Achievement in Special Visual Effects, and received ten further nominations including Outstanding Directing and Outstanding Writing.
entries.description: The television film that follows ordinary residents of Lawrence, Kansas, and Kansas City, Missouri, through and after a fictional nuclear exchange…
entries.text: The television film that follows ordinary residents of Lawrence, Kansas, and Kansas City, Missouri, through and after a fictional nuclear exchange between NATO and the Warsaw Pact, written by Edward Hume and directed by Nicholas Meyer, first broadcast on ABC on November 20, 1983. Watched by an estimated 100 million people in roughly 38.5 million households, among the largest audiences any American television film has ever drawn, it reportedly affected White House nuclear policy directly: President Reagan wrote in his diary that the film left him "greatly depressed," and later credited it, alongside other factors, with shaping his approach to the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty he signed with Soviet premier Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987.

entries.category: The Television Film and the Format-Defining Pilot
entries.name: Battlestar Galactica (2003 film)
entries.author: Michael Rymer
entries.awards: Won the 2003 Visual Effects Society Award for Outstanding Visual Effects in a Television Miniseries and the 2003 Saturn Award for Best Television Presentation, with further Emmy and Saturn Award nominations.
entries.description: The television film that reimagines Glen Larson's 1978 premise as a considerably darker miniseries pilot — the Cylons now nearly annihilate humanity…
entries.text: The television film that reimagines Glen Larson's 1978 premise as a considerably darker miniseries pilot — the Cylons now nearly annihilate humanity in a surprise nuclear strike, and several major characters are recast across genders from the original — written and executive produced by Ronald D. Moore and directed by Michael Rymer, first broadcast across two nights on the Sci Fi Channel beginning December 8, 2003. Functioning as a backdoor pilot rather than a stand-alone film, its combined 3.9 and 4.5 million viewers made it the strongest debut in the channel's history to that point, and Sci Fi ordered a thirteen-episode weekly series directly on the strength of the reception — closing, on the far side of a quarter century, the same pilot-to-series gamble Larson's original opened this category with.
